pointers.sentence: It adds one step to `SearchVectorExact`: its `process_lhs` wraps the left side in a `SearchVector`, with the right side's configuration if it has one; the inherited `process_rhs` wraps a right side that is not already a query in a `SearchQuery` with the vector's configuration; and `SearchVectorExact.as_sql` puts `"@@"` between them (`django/contrib/postgres/lookups.py:SearchLookup.process_lhs`, `django/contrib/postgres/search.py:SearchVectorExact`):

It adds one step to `SearchVectorExact`: its `process_lhs` wraps the left side in a `SearchVector`, with the right side's configuration if it has one; the inherited `process_rhs` wraps a right side that is not already a query in a `SearchQuery` with the vector's configuration; and `SearchVectorExact.as_sql` puts `"@@"` between them (`django/contrib/postgres/lookups.py:SearchLookup.process_lhs`, `django/contrib/postgres/search.py:SearchVectorExact`):

The lookup registered on it as `"exact"` is `SearchVectorExact`, so a filter by a plain string on a vector field, or on an annotation whose output is one, compares it with a `SearchQuery` in the vector's configuration, if it has one (`django/contrib/postgres/search.py:SearchVectorExact.process_rhs`).

Nothing in the module fills a vector column; the documentation suggests a trigger or a `GeneratedField` (`docs/ref/contrib/postgres/search.txt`), and an index over the vector ([PostgreSQL indexes and `ExclusionConstraint`](postgres-indexes.md)).
A weight, one of PostgreSQL's labels A to D, wraps the call in `"setweight"`, which labels that part's lexemes for the ranking (`django/contrib/postgres/search.py:SearchVector.as_sql`).

A configuration, a name or an expression such as an `F` of a column that holds one, becomes a `SearchConfig`, written cast to `"regconfig"` as the first argument of `"to_tsvector"` (`django/contrib/postgres/search.py:SearchConfig`).

Vectors combine with `+`, and only with each other. `SearchVectorCombinable` sets `ADD` to `"||"`, PostgreSQL's concatenation of vectors, and its `_combine` makes a `CombinedSearchVector` that keeps the left side's configuration, or raises `TypeError`: "SearchVector can only be combined with other SearchVector instances, got SearchQuery." (`django/contrib/postgres/search.py:SearchVectorCombinable._combine`). The combination's type comes from the table of combinable fields, where the module registers at import `"||"` between two `SearchVectorField`s as giving a `SearchVectorField` ([Expressions: `resolve_expression` and `as_sql`](../sql/expressions.md)).
Any other type raises `ValueError` (`django/contrib/postgres/search.py:SearchQuery.__init__`).

`Combinable` refuses `&` and `|` unless both sides are conditions (`django/db/models/expressions.py:Combinable.__and__`); `SearchQueryCombinable` defines them again to make a `CombinedSearchQuery` with PostgreSQL's `"&&"` or `"||"` between (`django/contrib/postgres/search.py:SearchQueryCombinable`).

It is a `Value` of one string, and its `as_sql` writes one parameter: the string with each character of `spec_chars_re` (the apostrophe, the backslash, the null character and `"[]()|&:*!@<>"`) made a space, spaces collapsed, and quoted as a string literal by the driver; then, after a colon, `"*"` for a prefix and the weight's letter, and `"!"` in front when inverted (`django/contrib/postgres/search.py:Lexeme.as_sql`, `django/contrib/postgres/search.py:psql_escape`, `django/contrib/postgres/search.py:quote_lexeme`).

Lexemes combine with `&` and `|` into a `CombinedLexeme`, which writes both sides into one string, so a whole tree is still one parameter; `~` on a combination applies De Morgan's theorem, as its comment says, swapping the operator and inverting both sides (`django/contrib/postgres/search.py:CombinedLexeme.__invert__`).

`CombinedSearchQuery` declares no `__invert__`, and the `NegatedExpression` that `Combinable.__invert__` makes needs an output field that no combination of two queries has (`django/db/models/expressions.py:NegatedExpression.resolve_expression`): filtering by `~(SearchQuery("pilot") & SearchQuery("boat"))` raised `FieldError`.
`Lexeme` is new (`docs/releases/6.0.txt`).

Weights, four numbers for the labels D, C, B and A in that order, go first, cast to `"float4[]"` by a `Cast` to an `ArrayField`; a normalization, an integer of flags, goes last (`django/contrib/postgres/search.py:SearchRank.__init__`).
Without weights the server uses its own, which the documentation gives as 0.1, 0.2, 0.4 and 1.0 (`docs/ref/contrib/postgres/search.txt`).

Its options, kept under PostgreSQL's names (`"StartSel"`, `"MaxWords"` and the rest) when given, are written by `SearchHeadline.as_sql` into one string parameter with the connection's `compose_sql`, which on PostgreSQL has the driver format each value through a cursor (`django/contrib/postgres/search.py:SearchHeadline.as_sql`, `django/db/backends/postgresql/psycopg_any.py:mogrify`).

`TrigramSimilarity` writes `"SIMILARITY"` of an expression and a string; `TrigramWordSimilarity` and `TrigramStrictWordSimilarity` write `"WORD_SIMILARITY"` and `"STRICT_WORD_SIMILARITY"` with the string first; the distances, `TrigramDistance`, `TrigramWordDistance` and `TrigramStrictWordDistance`, are written by their `arg_joiner` as the operators `"<->"`, `"<<->"` and `"<<<->"` (`django/contrib/postgres/search.py:TrigramBase`, `django/contrib/postgres/search.py:TrigramWordBase`).

The lookups `"trigram_similar"`, `"trigram_word_similar"` and `"trigram_strict_word_similar"`, registered by `PostgresConfig.ready` on the same two fields, are `PostgresOperatorLookup`s whose operators, `"%%"`, `"%%>"` and `"%%>>"`, are PostgreSQL's with the percent sign doubled for the driver (`django/contrib/postgres/lookups.py:TrigramSimilar`, [Lookups: `Lookup`, `BuiltinLookup` and the standard comparisons](../sql/lookups.md)).
